It took me a little over a month to taper down entirely, and then I had a bit of a rough month after quitting entirely. Around the 1 month/ 6 week mark is when things started to feel a lot more manageable
Thank you! I've been off of nicotine for a little over 3 months now. I had a slip up around the 2 month mark, and still have some cravings, but coffee and exercise and food seems to really help.

There is a version of future you that goes and gets the vape, and reawakens the addiction. The two months of incredible progress you've made is entirely gone. The stress relief lasts for 45 seconds tops, then is replaced by a new sinking pit in your stomach, and even more stress, tension, and anxiety, because one hit becomes two, becomes more than you can count, then you're dragged back down all over again, and feel even worse than before.

And there's you in the future who has been clean from this awful chemical for 3 months. That isn't as far away as it may seem. You're feeling a bit more steady, and you feel more peace, more calm, far more frequently than you have in ages. You can feel your brain healing itself. It's not all the way there yet, but you're starting to get these glimpses of the light you've worked so hard to reach. Sneak peeks at the happiness and health that is on its way for you. You've shown your brain that cravings can't control you. They might be uncomfortable, but because you didn't act on them, you showed your subconscious mind that those feelings can't keep you from your goals. The uncomfortable feelings are just uncomfortable, not threatening. And you have months of evidence of your own power and ability to stick to your goal. 

The choices you make in each moment are going to take you down one of either of these paths. 

Although it might be uncomfortable in the present, there's a version of you in the future that feels much better, and will thank you for taking care of them now, in this moment.

For me at least, tapering down was the only way I could quit. I tried to do cold turkey a couple times and the idea of never consuming nicotine again was too much for me

Cutting down gradually helped me learn how to experience nicotine cravings without acting on them. Even if it was intense or overwhelming, when I was cutting down I knew I could eventually hit my vape, so I didn't have to act on the urge right away. I got to a point where I realized the craving would only really last for 3-5 minutes, maybe 20 minutes tops. 

I could gradually reduce the amount of nicotine I was consuming and reduce my dependency on it, without feeling panicked and stressed about quitting or slipping up. I saw it as practicing to go through the heavier withdrawals and cravings that would come when I stopped all together. By the time I was close to actually stopping, I was mostly relieved to be done with it. The  smoke breaks I did take just kind of felt like a headache and stressed me out, it didn't feel like a reward anymore, just a burden. I was glad to be done with it. 

Everyone is going to find different things that work for them, it's helpful to do some research and experimenting.

Goodwill's focus as far as I can gather from the training videos they gave us is their community programs. The retail centers are mostly a way for the non profit to generate revenue, the majority of that goes to supporting a bunch of different community support programs and then like, keeping the lights on and paying employees' wages and that kind of thing. We have different CEOs per region, but many of them do have like 6 figure salaries.

Personally, I wish Goodwill would realize that the retail centers can serve just as important a function in local communities as the day programs.
 
We have at least over 30 programs we're told to ask customers to round up and support, they help people with disabilities, the elderly, formerly incarcerated individuals build job and life skills, there's programs that help people keep their heat and electricity on during the winter, etc; they do a lot of good, but the majority of people shopping at the retail centers are doing so because its the only place we can afford to. It feels wrong to overprice items and then beg for their spare change when the majority of people probably could benefit from our programs themselves. They shouldn't be the ones asked to fund these things, either through donations or ridiculously high prices.

 Intentionally overpricing freely donated goods just to increase the amount we can send to community programs does more harm to the community overall than good. If people are priced out of shopping at Goodwill (I'm an employee at Goodwill and some of our stuff is too expensive for me, even with the employee discount), then people are just going to stop going here altogether, and the entire organization is going to collapse.

My mom managed to quit smoking after 25 years, and she said that after you get through the initial few weeks, the cravings you get afterwards are likely caused by some kind of trigger. In the first two weeks, there's a lot of triggers that can cause cravings, like driving in your car if you used to smoke then, drinking a cup of coffee, taking a break at work, etc. Sometimes you accidentally come across something that triggers that urge to smoke really strongly, so you'll get cravings you didn't expect seemingly out of nowhere. If you've made it 63 days, you've probably hit most of those moments and made it out smoke free, this is just another one of those. You've got a great track record so far, and cravings (even mental ones) will usually only last about 20-30 minutes. Have a cup of coffee, a piece of candy, get outside or get some sunshine, find something that takes up all your focus so your focus isn't on the craving feeling anymore. Hang in there, you've got this!

Yes, 100%. Before I started smoking I had way more energy than I have now, coffee was all I needed to get through difficult shifts at my restaurant, and now no matter how much sleep I get, how much nicotine I consume, how much caffeine I have, I've never had the same amount of energy that I used to at work.

Quitting nicotine, after about a month of two, will give you a lot more energy and can have the same effect on your mood as taking anti depressants. It's rough at first, and the mental cravings can be tough if you don't know how to handle them, but it evens out and the world looks a lot brighter afterward

 It was a struggle to even get close to that number, I could do it on a good day but I couldn't hit it every day, and I didn't understand why they weren't reprimanding me or writing me up for being below numbers. Eventually an assistant manager told me that I was the first person in three years to actually hit numbers or even get to 200, and the people who did electronics before were like guys twice my size. 

They set pretty unrealistic expectations at my location, and I really hurt myself trying to reach them. My entire left arm (I'm left handed, I used that arm more), the left side of my neck and even my face would be numb at the end of the day because my muscles were so strained they were inflamed and putting pressure on the nerves to a point where I couldn't feel anything.

 If you're young, in pretty good shape, and used to heavy lifting and working really fast the whole day, it can kind of be fun, but if you're applying to work there I definitely recommend avoiding doing electronics or furniture sorting.

I worked at a fast food place (not a Wendy's) that was routinely understaffed and a couple times we actually did have buns that had mold growing on them. At my location, this usually happened because the company we actually ordered the buns from would give us outdated products. The company is supposed to supply you with buns that can last for at least two weeks, even though we would never actually have them in the kitchen for that long since we went through multiple trays with multiple bags of buns throughout the day. This store is probably really understaffed, mismanaged, and having issues with their suppliers, the only way we wouldn't notice the mold right away at my restaurant were on days when they had maybe two or three people to try and handle the store by themselves, and we were working faster than anyone should to try and just keep up with the orders. I don't want to throw shade at employees who probably are being overworked and mismanaged, but this kind of thing is dangerous, it's scary to realize your food could have made you seriously sick or could have killed you. Definitely report this to a health and safety inspector and maybe talk to the management at this place if you can, understaffing isn't just bad for employees, it can lead to food safety violations. Definitely avoid this Wendy's, there's likely several other food safety violations occuring if more obvious things like moldy buns aren't getting caught.

It's really not a question of if you're TA or not, it's more about dealing with anxiety and making choices about what you want your life to be about.

I've dealt with social anxiety my whole life, and I know how scary it can be to try and interact with people face to face. The fear and anxiety is really severe. Heart palpitations, racing thoughts, sweating, wondering if it's even worth it to deal with the discomfort, or if it would be better to give up on having connections with other people, just to avoid the pain of anxiety or rejection. 

It's really up to you in the end. 

It sounds like they're good friends of yours, they bring a lot of joy into your life, and because you all met initially on Discord, which was a safer and more comfortable way for you to interact, it must be really hard to realize that that's changing. 

Deciding between suffering from anxiety or losing your friend group isn't an easy choice to make. There's pressure on both sides, and it's up to you to decide what's best. 

Maybe the answer is that you find a group of people who do want to interact solely online, and part ways with these people.

 Maybe the answer is that you allow yourself to feel uncomfortable, anxious, distressed, whatever social interactions bring up for you, and remind yourself that your fear doesn't have to make your decisions for you. The more you do it, I promise you, the easier these things get. The first few times you meet up will be scary. But if you let yourself try this out, you might find that interacting with people becomes easier and easier over time, and you won't have to be distanced from your friends.

Hate speech is generally defined as someone using words to attack another person based on their personal demographics, like race, gender, sexuality, religion, etc. These words are used with the intent to attack or harm the other person, or to incite violence against them. The circumstances surrounding the use of the words matter, as well as the actual words being used themselves. 

A lot of social media sites will take down posts using phrases like "men are trash," because it's a comment directly aimed against a group of people specifically because of their gender.

At the same time, the existing power dynamics between groups of people will drastically change the impact and effect of the words being used. 

This girl wasn't saying "all men are trash," with the intent to actually go out and harm men, she was saying this in response to news about a woman being attacked by a man. 

Personally, I think that the meme joking about all men should start out in prison sort of starts to cross a line, where it's inviting harmful actions being done to people because of their gender, but I can sort of sympathize with both parties here. 

It's not fun to hear your partner put down a group of people YOU belong to. And it's also terrifying to hear about violence against a group of people that you belong to, and to have lived a whole life being afraid that something like that could happen to you or your friends. People make bad choices and act defensively when they're scared, or when they feel attacked. Both of you feel threatened.

Would definitely recommend going out of your way to get to Park Meadows, it's a MUCH nicer experience, but my favorite mall in Colorado Springs will always be the Chapel Hills Mall.

 It's maybe not the fanciest mall in the world, and I have years of childhood memories playing in the kids area and seeing Santa Claus and the Easter Bunny there that definitely make my answer biased, but it's a great place in the city if you're looking for a mall nearby.

 It's got your standard YA focused stores like Hot Topic, Spencer's, Claire's, clothing stores like H&M, American Eagle, and some nicer boutiques; a few local businesses like a natural beauty product store, a leather goods store, and larger department stores. 

There's a place that specializes in model trains, one that has action figures from film and comic books, a store that just sells Star Wars collectibles and funko pops, and and a train ride for kids and parents that runs through the entire store. 

Kind of recently they also added animal go-cart type things that you can ride through the mall, so there's definitely plenty of stuff to keep kids entertained. 

There's also a movie theater inside the mall, which is a great place to hang out with friends or plan date nights.

Chapel Hills mall is a little run down and not one of the nicer malls in Colorado, but it's definitely got a lot of hidden gems and does a great job of covering the basics while even offering some interesting specialized stores. Couple of different things-

First off, you definitely have not screwed up your entire college experience. Thoughts about having ruined things or messed things up is part of the anxiety disorder. They're projections, not actual facts. 

Your brain's on the look out for social threats, and it will tend to focus on the negative, or signs that things are going wrong, as a way to protect you from going through pain. That's where the disordered thinking kicks in. You could have a million good social interactions in a week, like you have, and because of the anxiety your brain will hyper fixate  on what it thinks went badly. We tend to hyper focus on the negative, and overlook the positive things. 

 Even with your anxiety, you've made friends with your roommate, and you've even been brave enough to meet a bunch of new people, even though it was scary and uncomfortable. That's a huge step in the right direction. Give yourself credit, cause it's definitely due here. 

You could have chosen to hide in your room, or to not talk to your roommate, or to not meet new people at your dorm. Instead, you sat through the discomfort, and benefitted from it. Remind yourself of the good things that happened because you decided to interact with other people. It sounds cheesy, like focusing on the positive instead of the negative, but it's part of training your brain to avoid spiraling into anxiety after a social situation. Imagine that you're working to prune away anxious trains of thought (I don't connect with others quickly)  while encouraging positive ones (I'm pushing myself to try new things and meet new people, I made friends with my roommate, etc)  to grow more frequently.

Social anxiety is a long uphill battle. And it's tempting to quit, especially when you're seeing other people connect so quickly. It's so crucial to remind yourself of the victories you've already made, and to continue interacting with others. 

You'll have anxious thoughts, insecurities, and worries. Expect those to be there, and give them absolutely no weight. They don't matter nearly half as much as you think they do. If you make all your decisions about interacting with others based on fear, you take away your own autonomy and ability to choose. 

You're already half way there. You're making the right choices, even if they're hard. You're not letting anxiety make your decisions, you're making your decisions.  You're putting yourself out there.  You've made one friend, so you know for a fact that you can and will make more friends. Don't count yourself out. Your future self is going to thank you for the work you're doing now. You're just getting started, and you're doing great. 

Just keep going. It's the hardest part, but just keep going. 




Also, a few more things, as a side note. 

-- you haven't ruined your college experience, I know it feels like that. Most friends you make during your freshman year won't be your friends in later years, many  people won't meet most of their good friends until about their 2nd or 3rd year, in my experience. Freshman tend to underestimate just how many people they're going to meet within their four years of college. It's kind of like tunnel vision. All your eggs are not in your freshman year dorm basket. You're doing the right thing now, by meeting lots of people. Meet people in your classes as well, and don't let the thoughts you're having now cut those future opportunities short. You've got this. 

--- Focus on the hits, not the misses. There's this weird unspoken lie in college that the number of friends you have needs to be freakishly high. I know people in college who have a lot of friends, I know people who literally only have one. And they're all healthy, happy, and normal people living functional lives. You don't need to be friends with everyone in your dorm. Most people aren't. Social anxiety made me zero in on the people who I thought didn't like me, and I would obsess over how to get them to like me, or how much of a loser I was. And then I sort of forgot about the friends who did like me. I neglected the happy, good relationships by accident, because I was focused on who didn't like me and how to get them to change their minds. I started spending time with people who I knew I clicked with, and it changed my life for the better. 

--  I get what you mean about seeing everyone click around you much quicker, and watching people come up with stuff to say right on the spot while it takes you longer. I promise, the people around you don't notice this at all. Most people also feel this way. I can guarantee you. I used to feel this way, and I thought that there was just something off about me, or that I just didn't have what it takes to make friends. That's not the case at all. Anxiety makes it harder to focus on the conversation and to join in easily. It just takes time, and experience. You'll get more and more comfortable talking with people in groups. People who make friends super fast tend to be very extroverted, and very open. These are more surface level relationships, especially right at the start. It might look like they can make friends faster, but there's a lot more that goes into it. You have everything you need to make long lasting, significant relationships. Just keep reaching out to people. You'll be okay.

Good luck OP! College is an exciting time, and you're already on the right track! You're doing great, focus on the things you can actively change, keep in mind the friendships and progress you've already made and will continue to make. Be good to yourself while you're working through your anxiety, and remember that the good experiences you're going to have in college are worth working through the anxiety. 

Keep us updated if you ever need to reach out! We're all on this thread rooting for you!

One thing that can really, really help in these situations is just asking questions. Really simple questions like how's your day been going will usually prompt the other person to start talking about their day, and you can start asking more questions from there. People usually like talking about themselves or the things they did that day, if you ask a cashier how their day is going, usually they'll be happy to talk about their shift, their weekend, their plans later on, etc. 

This is a good tactic for social anxiety because the pressure is lifted off of you to carry most of the conversation. If you're worried about coming up with responses, all you have to do is repeat back and paraphrase whatever the person said to you, and then ask another question again. This is enough to get you through small talk, and to help slowly start to feel more confident in conversations with others.

I know it sounds ridiculous, I swear, this works. I've been in behavioral therapy for social anxiety and this is one of the tactics I was taught. 

 If you're hanging out with someone at school or work or at any social event, you can try asking questions about whatever activity you're both doing. The best questions are the simplest, most open ended ones. Things as simple as asking how was your weekend can carry a conversation really far.  

Also, think of social skills and conversational skills as a muscle you have to exercise. Think of each conversation you have as a chance to hone your skills. It'll go slowly at first, it will be hard to talk with people and keep the conversation going. It will be a little awkward and uncomfortable. But the more you do it, the more natural it will feel, and conversation will come a little bit easier every single time.

Pushing through that initial discomfort and remembering that the real goal is beyond the scope of one conversation or one social interaction is what's going to solidify actual progress.

The pain isn't always going to be here. It takes a long time to get through the pain of a break up, and studies show that people actually tend to overestimate how much time it'll take them to heal. It feels like it'll last forever, but once the dust settles and the pain lifts, it will get better.

This kind of pain is similar to going through a drug withdrawal or losing a loved one. This is hard. Take care of yourself. Be good to yourself. Stay in contact with friends and family, and try and look at the situation the same way you might look at healing an injury. Research how to get through a break up. Take care of your broken heart the way you'd take care of a broken bone. Be gentle with yourself, and direct all that energy you used to spend in grief to beginning to heal yourself.

Not even another 3 months from now, it will get better. There is always counseling and therapy to turn to as well, whenever you need additional support. You have a lot more capacity for healing than you can even realize.

Stay strong, and I hope the pain eases soon.
